nodes.statement: Will AI cause mass unemployment in the U.S. within the next 15 years?
nodes.summary: Will AI cause mass unemployment in the U.S. within 15 years?

provenance.sourceRef: synthesized from all six research reports

nodes.label: Yes — it's already starting
nodes.statement: AI is already causing measurable, AI-caused employment displacement concentrated in early-career and AI-exposed white-collar work, and this will compound into a broad U.S. unemployment crisis within 15 years.
nodes.constituency: Labor economists documenting entry-level hiring collapse (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, Census researchers), frontier-lab leaders forecasting rapid capability growth, and journalists covering AI-attributed layoffs.
nodes.steelmanBasis: Two independently-designed studies (Stanford/ADP payroll data and Census QWI industry-state cells), using different data sources and different methods, both find a double-digit relative employment decline for early-career workers in AI-exposed occupations after controlling for firm-level and macro shocks — a convergence that is hard to wave away as a single adversarial source.

provenance.sourceRef: a-empirical-record.md §2 Entry-Level White-Collar Hiring; c-capability-forecasts.md §1 Measured Capability Trends

nodes.summary: Early-career workers in AI-exposed jobs are down 16% since 2022. Believers say that's the front edge of a crisis, not a blip.

nodes.label: No — we've panicked before
nodes.statement: The current alarm over AI and jobs repeats a 250-year pattern of failed technological-unemployment predictions; the observed early-career decline is substantially explained by the interest-rate cycle, the post-2021 tech correction, and offshoring, not AI, and historical reinstatement will again absorb displaced labor.
nodes.constituency: Economic historians and diffusion-skeptic researchers (Narayanan & Kapoor, Autor's task-based framework, Acemoglu's modest-TFP estimate) plus labor-market analysts pointing to confounds in the early-career data.
nodes.steelmanBasis: Every headline number in the displacement case has a live confound: Indeed's own data shows nearly half of the tech-postings decline predates ChatGPT, the Federal Reserve found no aggregate reduction in job postings at AI-adopting firms, and 250 years of automation — agriculture, ATMs, containerization — never produced permanent mass unemployment, because reinstatement and demand growth absorbed displaced labor even when specific cohorts suffered.

provenance.sourceRef: a-empirical-record.md §5 AI-Attributed Layoffs; b-theory-history.md §4 Steelman: This Time Is Like Last Time

nodes.summary: 250 years of machine-panic, and the economy kept inventing new work. Half the tech-hiring collapse predates ChatGPT.

nodes.label: Not fewer jobs — worse ones
nodes.statement: AI will not push headline U-3 unemployment into crisis territory, but it will reproduce the historical pattern in which a specific, identifiable cohort absorbs concentrated wage stagnation, occupational downgrading, and credential devaluation even as aggregate employment statistics look normal.
nodes.constituency: Labor economists studying wage structure and concentrated regional/occupational shocks (Acemoglu-Restrepo's wage-structure decomposition, the China-shock literature, Dallas Fed wage-growth researchers).
nodes.steelmanBasis: The historical record — Engels' pause, telephone operators, the China trade shock — shows the sharpest technology-driven harms have consistently shown up as wage stagnation and cohort-specific earnings loss rather than headline unemployment; defining 'mass unemployment' as U-3 above 10% and then declaring victory when it doesn't happen ignores exactly the channel through which past transitions actually hurt people.

provenance.sourceRef: b-theory-history.md §5 Middle Positions; h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed

nodes.summary: Unemployment stats stay calm while one identifiable cohort absorbs pay cuts, downgrading, and a broken career ladder.

nodes.label: Wrong question — who decides?
nodes.statement: Whether AI produces mass unemployment is not a fact waiting to be measured; it is a policy and governance outcome. The real disagreement is who gets to decide the pace and terms of AI deployment, and who bears the transition costs — questions evidence about exposure and capability cannot settle.
nodes.constituency: Labor unions and their bargaining precedents (WGA, SAG-AFTRA, ILA), algorithmic-management researchers (Dubal), and policy scholars focused on transition-cost allocation and worker voice.
nodes.steelmanBasis: Live, binding precedents already exist — WGA's 2023 MBA AI provisions, SAG-AFTRA's digital-replica consent requirements, the ILA's 2025 automation-protection agreement — showing that identical AI capability produces very different worker outcomes depending on who holds bargaining power over deployment, which is the actual lever available in the next 15 years regardless of how the empirical capability dispute resolves.

provenance.sourceRef: d-policy-normative.md PROCEDURAL: Who decides deployment terms?

nodes.summary: Whether AI 'causes' unemployment is a policy outcome, not a forecast. The real fight is over who sets the terms.

nodes.statement: Early-career workers in the most AI-exposed occupations have experienced a relative employment decline since 2022.
nodes.statusBasis: Two independently designed studies using different data (ADP payroll microdata; Census Quarterly Workforce Indicators) and different methods both find a double-digit relative decline for 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations, but both cover a short post-treatment window, the Stanford team's own broadest-controls specification pushes significant timing to 2024, and Strada's 2026 employer survey reports mixed expectations rather than a one-way collapse.

resolution.condition: a longer post-treatment panel and replication by an independent research team using a third administrative data source

nodes.statement: The early-career employment decline in AI-exposed occupations is caused by AI adoption rather than the interest-rate cycle, the tech-sector correction, or offshoring.
nodes.statusBasis: Stanford's follow-up specifically tested and rejected interest rates as a full explanation, but rival explanations (offshoring, the broader tech hiring freeze, which Indeed shows was already half-collapsed before ChatGPT) remain live and are not ruled out by the same data.

resolution.condition: linked employer-worker data with firm-time controls, AI adoption timing, occupation-level task automation measures, and worker reallocation outcomes settle attribution

nodes.summary: Is AI what broke entry-level hiring — or was it rates, the tech bust, and offshoring?

nodes.statement: Interest-rate increases and the broader tech-sector hiring correction do not fully explain the disproportionate decline in entry-level, AI-exposed employment.
nodes.statusBasis: Rests on a single follow-up note by the authors of the study whose result is at stake, untested by any independent team, and conceding statistical significance only from 2024 under the broadest controls.

nodes.statement: Nearly half of the decline in U.S. tech job postings from their peak occurred before ChatGPT's public release.
nodes.statusBasis: Indeed's own Hiring Lab analysis of its tech-postings index reports this directly and concludes there is no 'smoking gun' linking the plunge specifically to AI.

nodes.statement: A material share of the decline in U.S. junior white-collar hiring reflects offshoring to global capability centers in India and the Philippines rather than AI automation.
nodes.statusBasis: The corpus explicitly flags this as an unverified causal split: the scale of India's global-capability-center buildout over 2022-2026 makes the hypothesis plausible, but no public data links specific U.S. entry-level cuts to specific simultaneous offshore hiring in the same functions.

resolution.condition: firm-level data linking U.S. entry-level cuts to simultaneous India/Philippines/GCC hiring in the same functions; absent that, this remains unverified

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §2 Rival Hypothesis: Offshoring and Global Labor Arbitrage

nodes.statement: U.S. aggregate unemployment stayed below 4.5% through mid-2026, while labor-force participation declined from 62.3% to 61.5% between December 2022 and June 2026.
nodes.statusBasis: Direct BLS unemployment and labor-force-participation series show no strict U-3 mass-unemployment crisis through June 2026, but the participation decline means the macro record should not be summarized as simply normal under broader labor-market definitions.

nodes.statement: Firms facing improved AI capability respond primarily by reducing hiring and headcount growth rather than by expanding output or redesigning jobs to use the freed-up capacity.
nodes.statusBasis: This is an unstated mechanism assumption underlying the causal-attribution case: the observable data (hiring rates, headcount) cannot by itself distinguish 'AI reduced labor demand' from 'AI raised output per worker and firms chose to expand.' The corpus's own firm-level bridge evidence (Hampole et al.-style reallocation) is not decisive either way.

provenance.sourceRef: a-empirical-record.md §4 Firm-Level Experiments and Macro Estimates

resolution.condition: firm-level panels linking AI adoption to headcount, output, and pricing decisions over multiple years

nodes.summary: When AI makes a firm more productive, does it hire fewer people — or just sell more?

nodes.statement: 'Mass unemployment' should be defined as sustained U-3 unemployment above 10% for multiple quarters, rather than by wage collapse, labor-force participation decline, or underemployment.
nodes.statusBasis: The corpus's definitional-crux section lays out at least three live candidate definitions (strict U-3 above 10%, a stronger 15-20% Amodei-style crisis threshold, and a broader participation/wage/underemployment definition) with no consensus among the sides on which one settles the parent question.

resolution.condition: sides agree on a metric before forecasting: U-3 threshold and duration, employment-population ratio, U-6, prime-age participation, or entry-level career access

nodes.summary: What counts as 'mass unemployment' — are both sides even arguing about the same disaster?

nodes.statement: U.S. agricultural employment collapsed from roughly 41% of the workforce in 1900 to about 2% by 2000 without the economy settling into permanent mass unemployment.
nodes.statusBasis: Multiple converging historical data series (CEA archive, Federal Reserve long-run tables, USDA) document the same decline with no contrary account in the corpus; displaced agricultural labor moved into manufacturing and services over decades.

nodes.statement: During Britain's Industrial Revolution, output per worker rose substantially faster than real wages for several decades, a pattern known as the 'Engels' pause.'
nodes.statusBasis: Crafts' revised estimates (43.9% output-per-worker growth versus 27.1% real consumption-earnings growth, 1770-1840) and Allen's earlier, starker estimates both show the pattern, though the two studies differ on exact magnitude.

nodes.statement: Telephone operator employment fell 50-80% during AT&T's 1920-1940 mechanization of switching, and incumbent operators were more likely a decade later to be in lower-paying occupations or out of work, even though later cohorts' overall employment did not fall.
nodes.statusBasis: Feigenbaum and Gross's peer-reviewed QJE/NBER micro-historical study documents both halves of this result directly from AT&T personnel and Census data.

nodes.statement: Human comparative advantage is broad enough that new AI-complementary tasks will continue to emerge and reinstate labor demand, as happened after past automation waves.
nodes.statusBasis: This is Autor's central task-based prediction, directly disputed by the 'no remaining comparative advantage' argument, which holds that AI (unlike prior automation) can eventually perform the very new tasks that would otherwise reinstate labor demand.

resolution.condition: evidence that new, sizable labor-intensive task categories emerge after AI deployment and pay wages comparable to displaced work

nodes.summary: Will new kinds of work appear fast enough, as they always have before?

nodes.statement: If AI can eventually perform the same new tasks that would otherwise reinstate labor demand, the historical reinstatement mechanism will fail to operate for AI as it did for prior automation waves.
nodes.statusBasis: Korinek and Suh's formal model of AGI as the ability to perform all tasks humans can perform directly implies this; it is contested because it depends on unresolved questions about whether AI capability actually reaches that generality within the 15-year window.

provenance.sourceRef: b-theory-history.md §3 Steelman: This Time Is Different

resolution.condition: AI systems demonstrate broad autonomous task generality across novel, previously non-automated task categories rather than only within pre-specified domains

nodes.summary: What if AI can do the new jobs too?

nodes.statement: AI development is biased toward labor-substituting automation that saves labor cost or increases managerial control without generating comparably large productivity gains or new labor-intensive tasks.
nodes.statusBasis: This is Acemoglu and Restrepo's own theoretical 'so-so automation' claim; it is disputed by researchers who argue AI is already generating new complementary task categories (translation quality control, AI-output oversight roles) fast enough to avoid the so-so pattern.

resolution.condition: measured productivity gains at AI-adopting firms versus the rate of new labor-intensive task creation over the next decade

nodes.statement: Workers displaced from automated tasks can retrain and relocate into newly created tasks at a cost and delay small relative to the productivity gains.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the steelman assumption behind reinstatement-based optimism about AI: adjustment can be costly in absolute terms but still small relative to productivity gains if new tasks and targeted programs work well. The corpus's retraining evidence challenges this assumption by showing weak outcomes for ordinary programs, without proving that better-funded, employer-linked, AI-specific programs could not perform better.

resolution.condition: well-funded, targeted retraining programs evaluated at national AI-displacement scale show earnings and reemployment outcomes comparable to pre-displacement work

nodes.summary: Can displaced workers move into new work without lasting damage?

nodes.statement: Regionally concentrated trade-driven job loss (the China trade shock) produced elevated unemployment, reduced labor-force participation, and depressed wages in exposed local labor markets for at least a decade, even though the U.S. economy overall adjusted.
nodes.statusBasis: Autor, Dorn, and Hanson's peer-reviewed decomposition and their later persistence work both document depressed wages, participation, and employment in exposed local labor markets through 2019, with no contrary finding in the corpus.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

nodes.statement: Enterprise AI diffusion is currently slow because integration, data access, workflow redesign, worker trust, procurement, compliance, and liability constraints bind more tightly than raw model capability.
nodes.statusBasis: Narayanan and Kapoor's 'AI as Normal Technology' argument, backed by the Census finding that only 5.4% of U.S. businesses used AI in production as of 2024, makes this case; it is directly opposed by the fast-diffusion argument that software propagates through SaaS products without the physical-installation lag of prior general-purpose technologies.

resolution.condition: 2027-2028 Census BTOS or comparable surveys show whether production-workflow AI adoption crosses roughly 25-30% of U.S. firms

nodes.statement: Measured task-completion time horizons for frontier AI agents on software, ML, and cybersecurity tasks grew exponentially between 2019 and 2026, doubling roughly every seven months.
nodes.statusBasis: This is METR's own directly reported trend measurement (Time Horizon 1.1), not itself in dispute; what is disputed is whether the trend continues and what it implies for employment.

nodes.statement: Frontier AI agents' measured task-completion time horizon will continue doubling at roughly its 2025-2026 rate through 2028, extending AI's reach to multi-day and multi-week tasks within the 15-year window.
nodes.statusBasis: METR itself warns that its benchmark suite is saturating above roughly 16 hours, making the extrapolation past that point unreliable; the trend's continuation past the current benchmark ceiling is exactly what is disputed.

resolution.condition: by end-2028, independent time-horizon suites with mostly non-saturated tasks show 50% horizons above one work-week across software, research, browser, and office workflows

provenance.sourceRef: c-capability-forecasts.md §1 Measured Capability Trends; Propositions Still In Dispute #1

nodes.statement: Measured 50%-success time horizons for frontier AI models run roughly five- to tenfold longer than measured 80%-success time horizons for the same models.
nodes.statusBasis: This is a directly measured property of the published benchmark data (Claude Mythos preview: P50 1044.78 minutes versus P80 185.91; Claude Opus 4.6: P50 718.81 versus P80 69.87; GPT-5: P50 203.01 versus P80 38.31), not an interpretive claim.

provenance.sourceRef: g-timeline-symmetry.md §2 Source Hygiene And Forecast Ecosystem Disclosure

nodes.statement: Reliability at high success rates, not raw median task-completion capability, is the threshold that determines whether AI substitutes for employed labor.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the interpretive claim connecting the P50/P80 gap to employment relevance; it is disputed by those who argue that partial, supervised, or human-reviewed automation is already economically substitutive even at coin-flip reliability on the hardest tasks.

resolution.condition: 2027-2028 OSWorld-like and enterprise-agent evaluations show >80% completion on multi-hour workflows with low hallucination, no reward hacking, and auditable error recovery

nodes.statement: AI capability progress will plateau or narrow in scope because the effective stock of high-quality training text, compute-efficient scaling, and reliable long-context reasoning are approaching practical limits.
nodes.statusBasis: Epoch AI's own data-limit and data-movement-bottleneck estimates support this, but the corpus's balance review notes that the plateau case in the underlying capability report is sourced almost entirely to Epoch and an Anthropic research blog, giving the skeptical position no independent voice.

resolution.condition: post-2030 frontier model releases show whether new approaches (synthetic data, other modalities, algorithmic efficiency) sustain prior capability growth rates or whether progress visibly narrows

nodes.statement: AI capability evaluators such as METR, Epoch AI, AI Impacts, and the Forecasting Research Institute systematically favor short-timeline conclusions because of a shared funding cluster and intellectual milieu with AI-risk philanthropy.
nodes.statusBasis: The funders are disclosed (Coefficient/Open Philanthropy grants to FRI, Epoch, and AI Impacts, plus METR's access relationships with OpenAI and Anthropic), but the corpus finds no causal proof that this funding shaped conclusions; the claim is raised as a structural concern by the corpus's own adversarial balance review, not established.

provenance.sourceRef: g-timeline-symmetry.md §2 Source Hygiene And Forecast Ecosystem Disclosure

resolution.condition: a comparison of short-timeline forecasters' track records against non-AI-risk-funded forecasters on the same resolved benchmark questions

nodes.statement: Frontier AI labs' short-timeline predictions about transformative AI or AGI should be discounted for the labs' fundraising, recruitment, regulatory, and product incentives to make near-term AI capability seem urgent.
nodes.statusBasis: The corpus proposes this discount as reasonable given the labs' obvious conflict of interest, but cannot verify a systematic base rate that tech insiders overpredict their own technologies; the general claim is explicitly flagged as unverified even though the specific conflict of interest is undisputed.

provenance.sourceRef: c-capability-forecasts.md §4 Insider Claims vs Outside Views

resolution.condition: a base-rate dataset comparing frontier-tech insiders' predictions to outcomes across multiple technology cycles

nodes.statement: U.S. nonfarm business labor productivity growth from 2024 through mid-2026 has been running well above its 2005-2019 trend, consistent with AI-driven productivity gains already appearing in the aggregate data.
nodes.statusBasis: The raw productivity figures (3.0% in 2024, 2.1% in 2025, 2.2% year-over-year in 2026 Q2, versus a roughly 1.4-1.5% 2005-2019 trend) are uncontested BLS data, but whether three-plus years running about 50% above trend represents an AI-driven acceleration, or ordinary cyclical variation, is itself disputed.

resolution.condition: a multi-year decomposition of productivity growth into AI-attributable and non-AI-attributable components

nodes.statement: No unmistakable AI-driven productivity boom or broad payroll contraction is visible yet in aggregate U.S. economic data through mid-2026.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the corpus's own headline 'no macro signal yet' reading of the same productivity series; it sits in tension with the observation that 2024-2026 productivity growth is itself running well above its pre-2020 trend.

resolution.condition: the same productivity decomposition; this claim and its rival reading resolve together once the acceleration is attributed

nodes.statement: Occupational AI-exposure scores measure task overlap with AI capability, not realized employment displacement, because most exposed occupations combine automatable and non-automatable tasks.
nodes.statusBasis: The ILO explicitly frames generative AI's dominant near-term effect as task transformation rather than full job automation for this reason; this is a methodological point about what exposure indices measure, not itself contested in the corpus.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

nodes.statement: Clerical and administrative-support workers face material employment displacement risk from generative AI over the next 15 years.
nodes.statusBasis: This forward-looking risk claim follows from clerical work's status as the most AI-exposed occupational group, but is directly contested by the point that exposure measures task overlap rather than realized displacement, and by the observation that AI-exposed workers are on average better cushioned by pay and credentials than non-exposed workers.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

resolution.condition: clerical employment, hiring, and wage data over at least eight further quarters relative to matched lower-exposure occupations

nodes.statement: Clerical and administrative-support work is the occupational group with the highest generative-AI exposure globally.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the ILO's (Gmyrek, Berg, Bescond) directly reported exposure-index finding, unchallenged elsewhere in the corpus, because clerical tasks are heavily text-, record-, accounting-, and scheduling-based.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

nodes.statement: Women are exposed to generative AI at roughly two to three times the rate of men in high-income countries, driven by occupational segregation into clerical work rather than by any difference in ability.
nodes.statusBasis: The ILO's 2025 refined exposure index and 2026 gender brief converge on consistent ratios (a roughly 2.7x exposure ratio; 9.6% of female employment versus 3.5% of male employment in the highest-exposure category) and explicitly attribute the gap to occupational segregation.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

nodes.statement: Black workers and workers without a bachelor's degree are substantially more likely to experience job displacement than white workers and workers with a bachelor's degree, and displaced workers' earnings remain depressed for years afterward.
nodes.statusBasis: Brookings' PSID-based study finds Black workers 67% more likely and non-bachelor's-degree workers 67% more likely to experience displacement than their respective comparison groups, with earnings 25% lower a full decade after displacement; no contrary source appears in the corpus.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

nodes.statement: Workers in the most AI-exposed occupations are disproportionately higher-paid and more educated than workers in the least AI-exposed occupations.
nodes.statusBasis: Pew's O*NET-based analysis directly reports this ($33/hour versus $20/hour; bachelor's-degree workers more than twice as likely to be in the highest-exposure jobs), and it is not disputed elsewhere in the corpus.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

nodes.statement: High AI exposure among educated, higher-paid workers means those workers are better cushioned against displacement harm by savings, credentials, and remote-work options than lower-exposure, lower-paid workers would be.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the optimistic reading of the exposure-versus-pay correlation; it is directly disputed by the claim that the same credentials being deployed as cushioning are the asset AI is depreciating.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

resolution.condition: reemployment earnings and duration outcomes for displaced high-exposure, credentialed workers relative to displaced low-exposure workers

nodes.statement: If routine junior-analyst, coding, paralegal, and administrative tasks become automatable, the credential-to-experience pathway that converts education into a wage premium narrows, even for otherwise well-cushioned educated workers.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the direct rebuttal to the credential-cushioning claim; it is reinforced by Dallas Fed evidence that a one-standard-deviation increase in AI exposure is associated with a measurable reduction in wage growth specifically in occupations with zero experience premium, where credentials do not otherwise protect workers.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §1 Who Is Exposed: Gender, Race, Class

resolution.condition: the same reemployment earnings and duration data; this claim and its rival reading resolve together

nodes.summary: Is a degree still a shield — or exactly the thing AI devalues?

nodes.statement: Home health and personal care aide jobs are projected to be the single largest source of U.S. job growth from 2024 to 2034, adding about 740,000 jobs at a 2024 median wage of roughly $34,900.
nodes.statusBasis: This is BLS's own Employment Projections 2024-34 figure, the single most directly responsive federal dataset to a 15-year U.S. employment question, and is not disputed elsewhere in the corpus.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §4 Where the Jobs Actually Are and Will Be

nodes.statement: An economy in which displaced administrative or clerical workers move into home-health and personal-care jobs paying $30,000-$40,000 less per year has successfully 'adjusted' to AI displacement.
nodes.statusBasis: This is a value claim the corpus explicitly frames as unresolvable by wage-gap evidence alone: whether 'adjustment' means any reemployment at all, comparable earnings, comparable autonomy, or socially useful work paired with wage insurance is a question of what adjustment is for, not a measurable fact.

resolution.condition: agreement on whether adjustment means any reemployment, comparable earnings, comparable autonomy, or socially useful work with wage insurance

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §4 Where the Jobs Actually Are and Will Be; Revised Disagreement Proposition 4

nodes.summary: If an $80K office worker becomes a $35K care worker, did the economy 'adjust'?

nodes.statement: Care work resists AI automation because it is embodied, relational, mobile, and trust-heavy, making it a durable labor-demand absorber regardless of cognitive AI progress.
nodes.statusBasis: This is plausible given care work's physical and relational character, but the corpus does not test whether robotics or process automation will erode this resistance over the 15-year horizon, and it competes directly with unresolved capability-trajectory questions about how far AI-plus-robotics progress reaches by 2041.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §4 Where the Jobs Actually Are and Will Be

resolution.condition: robotics and process-automation progress in home-health and personal-care settings over the next decade

nodes.statement: For most currently employed U.S. workers, the dominant AI-at-work experience over the next 15 years will be algorithmic management — automated scheduling, monitoring, quota-setting, and personalized pay — rather than outright job loss.
nodes.statusBasis: This is proposed as a reframing of the unemployment question itself; it has not yet been measured against AI-attributed layoff data at scale, though the mechanism (algorithmic wage-setting, warehouse monitoring) is independently well documented.

resolution.condition: worker surveys and administrative data show growth in automated scheduling, quota, pay, monitoring, and evaluation systems exceeding AI-attributable layoffs

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §3 The Labor the Corpus Couldn't See

nodes.statement: Data annotation, content moderation, and RLHF labeling are themselves a form of AI production work, employing an estimated global workforce in the millions, much of it low-wage and concentrated in the Global South.
nodes.statusBasis: Fairwork's cloudwork report and Appen's contributor-count figures converge on scale even though precise headcounts vary by source, and documented conditions (Kenyan Sama workers paid $1.32-$2/hour to review graphic content) are corroborated by multiple independent investigations.

provenance.sourceRef: h-workers-distribution-geography.md §3 The Labor the Corpus Couldn't See

nodes.statement: The "700 full-time agents" workload-equivalence figure for Klarna AI-assistant coverage does not establish that 700 employee positions were eliminated.
nodes.statusBasis: Klarna's own later actions confirm this reading: in May 2025 its CEO said the cost-cutting push had gone too far and the firm began recruiting human agents, while Klarna's own statement said it never stopped using outsourced agents even during the AI-first push.

nodes.statement: U.S. retraining programs such as Trade Adjustment Assistance have shown modest-to-negative earnings and employment effects for participants relative to matched comparison workers.
nodes.statusBasis: Mathematica's national TAA evaluation and the Department of Labor's CLEAR review both rate the earnings, wage, and employment evidence unfavorable, despite favorable effects on education and skills received.

nodes.statement: Better-designed, targeted, employer-linked, long-horizon workforce programs can meaningfully improve displaced workers' earnings and employment, even though generic short retraining programs mostly do not.
nodes.statusBasis: The WIA Gold Standard randomized evaluation found that staff-assisted intensive services increased earnings 7%-20%, while evidence on training itself was inconclusive within 30 months. That supports targeted case management, not generic retraining or effectiveness at the scale a national AI-displacement emergency would require.

resolution.condition: evaluation of a well-funded, AI-displacement-specific workforce program at national scale

nodes.summary: Could retraining actually work if it were done seriously — or is the record damning?

nodes.statement: Existing UBI and guaranteed-income pilots tested modest-to-moderate cash transfers in labor markets where jobs still existed, not in an economy experiencing AI-scale labor-demand collapse.
nodes.statusBasis: This scope limitation is a matter of research design that the corpus itself states directly: these trials can inform labor-supply, spending, and wellbeing effects, but cannot prove whether a national UBI would be fiscally sustainable, inflation-neutral, or adequate if AI caused a broad labor-demand collapse.

nodes.statement: Unconditional cash transfers modestly reduce recipients' labor-force participation and hours worked relative to controls.
nodes.statusBasis: OpenResearch's public summary and its NBER revision report different magnitudes for the same trial (2 percentage points/1.3 fewer hours versus 4.1 percentage points/1-2 fewer hours), while Stockton's SEED pilot found increased full-time employment among recipients relative to controls, so the direction is not uniform across the UBI evidence base.

resolution.condition: additional randomized UBI trials with consistent methodology across different labor-market conditions

nodes.statement: AI developers and deployers who profit from labor displacement owe wage insurance, retraining, severance, relocation, or public contributions to the workers whose displacement they caused.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the polluter-pays position in the corpus's own framing; evidence can estimate displacement, profits, and incidence, but cannot settle the moral boundary between innovation and compensable harm, which is exactly what this claim asserts.

resolution.condition: evidence can estimate displacement, profits, and capacity to pay, but cannot determine whether displacement is a compensable externality or ordinary market change

provenance.sourceRef: d-policy-normative.md NORMATIVE: Who owes transition costs?

nodes.statement: AI-driven productivity gains are ordinary market competition; firms owe only compliance with existing labor law, and compensation for displaced workers belongs to the general tax-and-transfer system rather than to AI firms specifically.
nodes.statusBasis: This is the market-process position directly opposed to the polluter-pays claim in the corpus's own framing of the dispute; both are stated as live, evidence-independent normative positions.

provenance.sourceRef: d-policy-normative.md NORMATIVE: Who owes transition costs?

resolution.condition: evidence can estimate displacement, profits, and capacity to pay, but cannot determine whether displacement is a compensable externality or ordinary market change

nodes.statement: Workers should have bargaining or veto rights over the terms of AI deployment in their workplaces before jobs are redesigned.
nodes.statusBasis: Live precedents exist on the labor-side-governance position: the WGA's 2023 MBA provisions bar AI from reducing writer credit or compensation, SAG-AFTRA requires informed consent and compensation for digital replicas, and the ILA's 2025 agreement won automation protections after a 2024 strike.

resolution.condition: resolved by allocating decision rights through collective bargaining law, contract precedent, or regulation, not by evidence or values converging

provenance.sourceRef: d-policy-normative.md PROCEDURAL: Who decides deployment terms?

nodes.summary: Should workers get a vote on how AI is deployed in their own jobs?

nodes.statement: Firms must retain managerial authority to adopt productivity-enhancing AI tools, subject only to existing law and contract, without new labor-side veto rights over deployment decisions.
